claim: Among Danio fishes, some species develop erythrophores, pigment cells that contain red ketocarotenoids.
source: Among Danio fishes, some species develop erythrophores, pigment cells that contain red ketocarotenoids, whereas other species, like zebrafish (D. rerio) only have yellow xanthophores.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analysis and imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Zebrafish (D. rerio) only have yellow xanthophores and lack erythrophores.
source: Among Danio fishes, some species develop erythrophores, pigment cells that contain red ketocarotenoids, whereas other species, like zebrafish (D. rerio) only have yellow xanthophores.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and confirmed by phylogenetic survey in Figure 1B.

claim: Erythrophores in the fin of D. albolineatus share a common progenitor with xanthophores.
source: We show that erythrophores in the fin of D. albolineatus share a common progenitor with xanthophores and maintain plasticity in cell fate even after differentiation.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis and fate mapping experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Erythrophores and xanthophores maintain plasticity in cell fate even after differentiation.
source: We show that erythrophores in the fin of D. albolineatus share a common progenitor with xanthophores and maintain plasticity in cell fate even after differentiation.
evidence: Demonstrated by regeneration experiments showing erythrophore to xanthophore conversion in Figure 5.

claim: The predominant ketocarotenoid that confers red coloration to erythrophores is astaxanthin.
source: We further identify the predominant ketocarotenoids that confer red coloration to erythrophores and use reverse genetics to pinpoint genes required for the differentiation and maintenance of these cells.
evidence: Identified by HPLC analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The intensity of red or orange coloration has been associated with mating preferences in a variety of species.
source: For example, the intensity of red or orange coloration, or the area over which it occurs, has been associated with mating preferences in a variety of species (Milinski and Bakker, 1990; Hill, 1991; Houde, 1997; Grether, 2000; Takahashi, 2018; Ansai et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Conspicuous coloration that makes an individual attractive can make it more vulnerable to predators.
source: and in some cases the very conspicuousness that makes an individual attractive can make it more vulnerable to predators (Endler, 1980; Godin and McDonough, 2003; Johnson and Candolin, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Red or orange coloration can be associated with aggressive interactions.
source: Red or orange coloration can also be associated with aggressive interactions (Evans and Norris, 1996; Pryke and Griffith, 2006; Dijkstra et al., 2008) and warning coloration (Brodie and Brodie, 1980; Stevens and Ruxton, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Red, orange, and yellow coloration is often mediated by the accumulation of carotenoids.
source: Red, orange, and yellow coloration is often mediated by the accumulation of carotenoids, fat-soluble compounds that are synthesized by plants and some fungi and bacteria, and obtained by animals via their diet and then subsequently modified (Bagnara and Matsumoto, 2006; McGraw, 2006; Svensson and Wong, 2011; Sefc et al., 2014; Strange, 2016; Toews et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Carotenoids are fat-soluble compounds synthesized by plants and some fungi and bacteria.
source: Red, orange, and yellow coloration is often mediated by the accumulation of carotenoids, fat-soluble compounds that are synthesized by plants and some fungi and bacteria, and obtained by animals via their diet and then subsequently modified (Bagnara and Matsumoto, 2006; McGraw, 2006; Svensson and Wong, 2011; Sefc et al., 2014; Strange, 2016; Toews et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Animals obtain carotenoids via their diet and then subsequently modify them.
source: Red, orange, and yellow coloration is often mediated by the accumulation of carotenoids, fat-soluble compounds that are synthesized by plants and some fungi and bacteria, and obtained by animals via their diet and then subsequently modified (Bagnara and Matsumoto, 2006; McGraw, 2006; Svensson and Wong, 2011; Sefc et al., 2014; Strange, 2016; Toews et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: More than a thousand naturally occurring carotenoids are known.
source: More than a thousand naturally occurring carotenoids are known, and their basic structure consists of 40 carbon atoms derived from four terpene molecules (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about carotenoid diversity.

claim: The basic structure of carotenoids consists of 40 carbon atoms derived from four terpene molecules.
source: More than a thousand naturally occurring carotenoids are known, and their basic structure consists of 40 carbon atoms derived from four terpene molecules (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing carotenoid structures.

claim: Carotenoids contain a system of conjugated double bonds that absorb light in the visible range.
source: Carotenoids contain a system of conjugated double bonds that absorb light in the visible range; the greater the length of the conjugated system, the more red-shifted the absorption.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carotenoid chemistry.

claim: The greater the length of the conjugated system in carotenoids, the more red-shifted the absorption.
source: Carotenoids contain a system of conjugated double bonds that absorb light in the visible range; the greater the length of the conjugated system, the more red-shifted the absorption.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carotenoid chemistry.

claim: Yellow carotenoids such as β-carotene or zeaxanthin have a total of 11 conjugated double bonds.
source: Yellow carotenoids, such as β-carotene or zeaxanthin, have a total of 11 conjugated double bonds, whereas red carotenoids, such as astaxanthin, have a total of 13 due to the addition of ketone groups in the 4 and 4' positions of the terminal rings of the molecule (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Red carotenoids such as astaxanthin have a total of 13 conjugated double bonds due to the addition of ketone groups in the 4 and 4' positions of the terminal rings of the molecule.
source: Yellow carotenoids, such as β-carotene or zeaxanthin, have a total of 11 conjugated double bonds, whereas red carotenoids, such as astaxanthin, have a total of 13 due to the addition of ketone groups in the 4 and 4' positions of the terminal rings of the molecule (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Many animal species possess endogenous 'ketolase' activity that can add ketones to diet-derived yellow carotenoids to produce red ketocarotenoids.
source: Many animal species possess endogenous 'ketolase' activity, and thus can add ketones to diet-derived yellow carotenoids to produce red ketocarotenoids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carotenoid metabolism in animals.

claim: The final color displayed by an animal reflects the specific carotenoids absorbed in the gut, transported to peripheral tissues, and chemically modified to achieve specific light-absorptive properties.
source: The final color displayed by an animal reflects the specific carotenoids absorbed in the gut, transported to peripheral tissues, and chemically modified to achieve specific light-absorptive properties.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carotenoid-based coloration.

claim: Carotenoids have important functions as vitamin A precursors, as antioxidants, and as regulators of a variety of cellular functions.
source: Carotenoids also have important functions as vitamin A precursors, as antioxidants, and as regulators of a variety of cellular functions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carotenoid functions.

claim: The multifunctionality of carotenoids and the need to obtain them from the environment have contributed to the notion that carotenoids in the integument can serve as an honest signal of prospective fitness.
source: The multifunctionality of carotenoids, and the need to obtain them from the environment, have contributed to the notion that carotenoids in the integument can serve as an honest signal of prospective fitness, to mates or rivals (Endler, 1980; Weaver et al., 2017; Weaver et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Of 17 Danio species assessed, 14 had erythrophores.
source: Of 17 Danio species assessed, 14 had erythrophores indicating this cell type is common and most likely was present in the common ancestor of all Danio species (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Based on direct observation and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Erythrophores are common in Danio species and most likely were present in the common ancestor of all Danio species.
source: Of 17 Danio species assessed, 14 had erythrophores indicating this cell type is common and most likely was present in the common ancestor of all Danio species (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic distribution shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the anal fin of adult D. albolineatus, red erythrophores are located proximally and are separated from the more distal yellow xanthophores by a narrow stripe of melanophores.
source: In the anal fin of adults, red erythrophores were located proximally and were separated from the more distal yellow xanthophores by a narrow stripe of melanophores (Figure 2A).
evidence: Directly observed and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Erythrophores are present in both sexes of D. albolineatus but are more deeply and consistently red in males than females.
source: Although erythrophores were present in both sexes, the cells were more deeply and consistently red in males than females and we therefore focused on males at stages when sexes were distinguishable (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Directly observed and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Male D. albolineatus older than 1 year often lack fin stripe melanophores.
source: Male fish older than 1 year often lacked fin stripe melanophores, indicating that some pattern remodeling continues even after sexual maturation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Directly observed and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Erythrophores occur at lower densities than xanthophores in D. albolineatus fins.
source: As compared to xanthophores, erythrophores occur at lower densities and were more likely to be binucleated (Figure 2B, middle and right panels; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Erythrophores are more likely to be binucleated than xanthophores.
source: As compared to xanthophores, erythrophores occur at lower densities and were more likely to be binucleated (Figure 2B, middle and right panels; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: Directly observed and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Binucleation is a characteristic associated with a mature state of differentiation in stripe melanophores of zebrafish.
source: a characteristic associated with a mature state of differentiation in stripe melanophores of zebrafish (Saunders et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Erythrophores autofluoresce in red whereas xanthophores autofluoresce in green under epifluorescence.
source: Erythrophores and xanthophores had different spectra under epiflourescence. Erythrophores autofluorescenced in red (displayed in magenta) whereas xanthophores autofluoresced in green.
evidence: Directly observed and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Hue values under brightfield illumination are correlated with ratios of red to green autofluorescence (R2 = 0.92, p < 0.0001).
source: Hue values under brightfield illumination were correlated with ratios of red to green autofluorescence (R2 = 0.92, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Colors of cells vary across the proximodistal axis of the D. albolineatus fin.
source: Colors of cells varied across the proximodistal axis of the fin, shown as relative position with fin base at 0 and fin tip at 1.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Erythrophores in proximal regions are distinct in both fluorescence ratio and visible hue from xanthophores in distal regions.
source: Erythrophores in proximal regions were distinct in both fluorescence ratio and visible hue from xanthophores in distal regions though some intergradation was evident in middle regions, near the melanophore stripe.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E.

claim: During the larva-to-adult transformation, ratios of red to green autofluorescence diverge between prospective erythrophore and xanthophore regions.
source: During the larva-to-adult transformation, ratios of red to green autofluorescence diverged between prospective erythrophore and xanthophore regions.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The first pigmented cells in the anal fin of D. albolineatus are lightly melanized melanophores.
source: The first pigmented cells in the anal fin were lightly melanized melanophores.
evidence: Observed during developmental imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Orange xanthophore-like cells appear after melanophores in the developing anal fin.
source: Subsequently, orange xanthophore-like cells appear that were pale and had smaller areas of visible pigment than mature erythrophores and xanthophores (Figure 2B, left panel; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed during developmental imaging shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Early orange cells autofluoresce in both red and green channels.
source: These early orange cells autofluoresced in both red and green channels, consistent with their appearance in brightfield (Figure 2F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F.

claim: During later development, cells in proximal regions become increasingly red whereas cells in distal regions become increasingly yellow.
source: During later development, however, cells in proximal regions were increasingly red whereas cells in distal regions were increasingly yellow.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Cell densities gradually diverge between proximal and distal regions during development.
source: Cell densities gradually diverged between proximal and distal regions as well (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In D. albolineatus injected with CRISPR/Cas9 reagents targeting scarb1, wild-type clones most often contained both red cells and yellow cells.
source: In D. albolineatus injected with high efficiency AltR CRISPR/Cas9 reagents targeting scarb1, wild-type clones most often contained both red cells and yellow cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When aox5:palmEGFP was injected at limiting dilutions, labeled cells were restricted to narrow regions along the anterior–posterior axis, consistent with derivation from single clones.
source: When we injected an aox5 reporter transgene at limiting dilutions to express membrane-targeted EGFP, labeled cells were restricted to narrow regions along the anterior–posterior axis, consistent with derivation from single clones observed in other contexts (Tu and Johnson, 2010; Singh et al., 2014; Spiewak et al., 2018).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 3B, with comparison to prior literature.

claim: In presumptive clones labeled with aox5:palmEGFP, erythrophores and xanthophores were almost always co-labeled.
source: Such cells occurred on the body and fin, and in these presumptive clones, erythrophores and xanthophores were almost always co-labeled (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with a common progenitor for erythrophores and xanthophores.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells on the body had converted and unconverted nucEosFP fluorophore, whereas cells in the fin had only unconverted fluorophore.
source: We found that cells on the body had converted and unconverted fluorophore, whereas cells in the fin had only unconverted fluorophore, consistent with initiation of aox5 expression only after progenitors had colonized the fin (Figure 3C).
evidence: Experimental result from photoconversion experiment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Photoconversion and repeated imaging failed to reveal cells that translocated from body to fin.
source: Such labeling failed to reveal cells that translocated from body to fin, although it did reveal numerous cells that acquired aox5 expression when already in the fin (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental result from repeated photoconversion experiment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Progenitors migrate to the fin, become specified for erythrophore or xanthophore lineages within the fin, and then contribute to both populations as they proliferate.
source: Together these observations suggest that progenitors migrate to the fin, become specified for erythrophore or xanthophore lineages within the fin, and then contribute to both populations as they proliferate to populate the proximal–distal axis during fin outgrowth.
evidence: Inferred from photoconversion experiments in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: At 7.0 mm SL, only unpigmented nucEosFP+ cells were present in the developing fin.
source: At 7.0 mm SL, only unpigmented nucEosFP+ cells were present (Figure 4A, top).
evidence: Directly observed and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Proximally located cells at 7.0 mm SL tended to remain in the proximal region where erythrophores develop.
source: Preliminary observations indicated that proximally located cells tended to remain in the proximal region where erythrophores develop, so we photoconverted cells in distal regions that might become more broadly distributed.
evidence: Preliminary observation from fate mapping experiments.

claim: Clones from unpigmented cells at 7.0 mm SL consisted of erythrophores if daughter cells remained relatively proximal, or both erythrophores and xanthophores if daughter cells became distributed across the proximodistal axis.
source: Resulting clones consisted of erythrophores if daughter cells remained relatively proximal as the fin grew out, or both erythrophores and xanthophores if daughter cells became distributed across the proximodistal axis (Figure 4B and C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental result from photoconversion fate mapping shown in Figure 4B, C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 7.5 mm SL, many nucEosFP+ cells had acquired a pale orange color.
source: At 7.5 mm, many nucEosFP+ cells had acquired a pale orange color (Figure 4A, bottom)
evidence: Directly observed and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Initially proximal orange cells at 7.5 mm SL generated only erythrophores, whereas initially distal orange cells could generate clones of only erythrophores, both erythrophores and xanthophores, or only xanthophores, depending on where daughter cells were distributed.
source: Similar to unpigmented cells, however, initially proximal orange cells generated only erythrophores, whereas initially distal orange cells could generate clones of only erythrophores, both erythrophores and xanthophores, or only xanthophores, depending on where daughter cells were distributed (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental result from photoconversion fate mapping shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At 8.5 mm SL, still-unpigmented nucEosFP+ cells near the distal fin tip generated distal clones restricted to a xanthophore fate.
source: Finally, at 8.5 mm we found that still-unpigmented nucEosFP+ cells near the distal fin tip generated distal clones restricted to a xanthophore fate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental result from photoconversion fate mapping shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Individual unpigmented cells and early-developing orange cells in the fin can generate both erythrophores and xanthophores, depending on initial location and where progeny localize.
source: These results show that individual unpigmented cells and early-developing orange cells in the fin can generate both erythrophores and xanthophores, depending on initial location and where progeny localize.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from photoconversion fate mapping experiments in Figure 4.

claim: During fin regeneration, small groups of cells having paler red or orange coloration were sometimes observable where individual cells of deep red coloration had been found.
source: As regeneration proceeded, small groups of cells having paler red or orange coloration, were sometimes observable where individual cells of deep red coloration had been found, suggestive of proliferation and dilution of pre-existing pigments.
evidence: Observed during repeated imaging through regeneration shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Later in regeneration, only yellow cells were found in locations where deep red erythrophores had previously been observed.
source: Later, only yellow cells were found in these same locations.
evidence: Observed during repeated imaging through regeneration shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Many erythrophores divided to replenish their complement in proximally regenerating tissue.
source: Many erythrophores divided to replenish their complement in proximally regenerating tissue, and a few erythrophores differentiated from unpigmented precursors, as indicated by the presence, or absence of photoconverted nucEosFP, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Experimental result from photoconversion regeneration experiment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Some initially marked erythrophores came to occupy more distal regions and were indistinguishable from regenerative xanthophores 36–51 days post-amputation.
source: Additionally, some initially marked erythrophores came to occupy more distal regions and were indistinguishable from regenerative xanthophores that had developed from unpigmented progenitors even 36–51 days post-amputation (Figure 5C).
evidence: Experimental result from photoconversion regeneration experiment shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Erythrophores can reduce pre-existing red pigment as cells divide and fail to accumulate new red pigments once proliferation has ceased.
source: These findings suggest a reduction in pre-existing red pigment as cells divide, and a failure to accumulate new red pigments once proliferation has ceased.
evidence: Inferred from regeneration experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Mapping D. albolineatus sequencing reads to the zebrafish genome identified 18,050 expressed genes.
source: Mapping D. albolineatus sequencing reads to the zebrafish genome identified 18,050 expressed genes.
evidence: Result from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Transcripts of 162 genes were more abundant in proximal erythrophore-containing tissue.
source: Transcripts of 162 genes were more abundant in proximal erythrophore-containing tissue, whereas transcripts of 200 genes were more abundant in distal xanthophore-containing tissue (q < 0.05; fold-changes = 0.4–6.8) (Figure 6A and B; Supplementary file 1—Table 1).
evidence: Result from RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Transcripts of 200 genes were more abundant in distal xanthophore-containing tissue.
source: Transcripts of 162 genes were more abundant in proximal erythrophore-containing tissue, whereas transcripts of 200 genes were more abundant in distal xanthophore-containing tissue (q < 0.05; fold-changes = 0.4–6.8) (Figure 6A and B; Supplementary file 1—Table 1).
evidence: Result from RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Of 25 target genes derived from RNA-seq, three yielded mutants with defects in pigmentation.
source: Of 25 targets derived from RNA-seq, three yielded mutants with defects in pigmentation.
evidence: Result from CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis screen.

claim: In wild-type D. albolineatus, fin tissue containing erythrophores is markedly enriched for the red ketocarotenoid astaxanthin.
source: In the wild type, fin tissue containing erythrophores was markedly enriched for the red ketocarotenoid astaxanthin; additional peaks had profiles consistent with other ketocarotenoids (Figure 7A, peak 3; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1—Table 4).
evidence: Result from HPLC analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fin tissue containing xanthophores lacks astaxanthin and instead contains yellow zeaxanthin.
source: Fin tissue containing xanthophores lacked astaxanthin and instead contained yellow zeaxanthin (peak 10), similar to zebrafish xanthophores (Saunders et al., 2019), as well as additional peaks characteristic of other yellow xanthophyll carotenoids.
evidence: Result from HPLC analysis shown in Figure 7A, with comparison to prior literature.

claim: Homozygous scarb1 mutants lack red and yellow coloration and carotenoids are not detectable.
source: We isolated two alleles, scarb1vp38ac1 (V84Δ16X) and scarb1vp38ac2 (V84X), and found that scarb1vp38ac1/vp38ac2 individuals had a phenotype concordant with that of F0 mosaics (Figure 3A): they lacked color in the visible range and lacked carotenoids detectable by HPLC (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A; Supplementary file 1—Table 4).
evidence: Experimental result from mutant analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The absence of residual red or yellow coloration in scarb1 mutants suggests that pteridine pigments do not contribute to visible color in these cells.
source: The absence of residual red or yellow coloration suggested that pteridine pigments do not contribute to visible color in these cells, as they do in some other species (Goodrich et al., 1941; Matsumoto and Obika, 1968; Grether et al., 2001; Weiss et al., 2012; Olsson et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from scarb1 mutant phenotype, with comparison to other species.

claim: Targeting of differentially expressed genes known to function in pteridine synthesis did not yield visible pigmentation defects in F0 mosaics.
source: Moreover, targeting of differentially expressed genes known to function in pteridine synthesis did not yield visible pigmentation defects in F0 mosaics (erythrophore region: spra, xdh; xanthophore region: aox5; Supplementary file 1—Tables 1 and 4).
evidence: Result from CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis screen.

claim: Pteridine pigments are detectable histologically in erythrophores and xanthophores.
source: Pteridine pigments were detectable histologically in erythrophores and xanthophores, however, and could be visible to fish in the UV range (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Shown by UV autofluorescence in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Mutants for cyp2ae2 and bdh1a lack overt red coloration.
source: Mutants for two genes, cyp2ae2 (FO904880.1) and bdh1a (zgc:113142), lacked overt red coloration (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Experimental result from mutant analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Densities of erythrophores and xanthophores in cyp2ae2 and bdh1a mutants do not differ significantly from wild-type.
source: although densities of erythrophores and xanthophores did not differ significantly from wild-type (Figure 7F).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 7F.

claim: cyp2ae2 and bdh1a have transcripts that are more abundant in fin tissue containing erythrophores than xanthophores.
source: Both genes had transcripts that were more abundant in fin tissue containing erythrophores than xanthophores (log2 fold-changes = 4.9, 2.1; q = 9.6E-23, 8.9E-8; Figure 6).
evidence: Result from RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: cyp2ae2 and bdh1a are expressed in erythrophores.
source: We confirmed by RT-PCR that both genes were expressed in erythrophores picked manually by micropipette from dissociated fin tissue (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Confirmed by RT-PCR shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: cyp2ae2 encodes an enzyme within the large family of cytochrome P450 monooxygenases.
source: cyp2ae2 encodes an enzyme within the large family of cytochrome P450 monooxygenases (Kirischian et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CYP2J19 is essential for red coloration in 'red factor' canary and zebra finch.
source: A related gene encoding a different P450 family member, CYP2J19, is essential for red coloration in 'red factor' canary (Lopes et al., 2016) and zebra finch (Mundy et al., 2016), and likely has similar roles in other birds and turtles (Twyman et al., 2016; Twyman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CYP2J19 expression is testosterone-dependent.
source: CYP2J19 expression is testosterone-dependent (Khalil et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CYP2J19 is believed to play an essential role in the conversion of yellow carotenoids like zeaxanthin into red ketocarotenoids like astaxanthin.
source: and its product is believed to play an essential role in the conversion of yellow carotenoids like zeaxanthin into red ketocarotenoids like astaxanthin (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Orthologs of CYP2J19 appear to be restricted to birds and turtles.
source: Orthologs of CYP2J19 appear to be restricted to birds and turtles (Twyman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: cyp2ae2 is likely orthologous to cyp2ae1 loci of other teleosts by sequence similarity and chromosomal position.
source: Reciprocally, cyp2ae2 (FO904880.1) is clearly a member of the cyp2 family, and is likely orthologous to cyp2ae1 loci of other teleosts by sequence similarity and chromosomal position, yet no clear orthologues of this gene are present in amniotes (Ensembl Release 103) (Kirischian et al., 2011; Yates et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and database searches.

claim: No clear orthologues of cyp2ae2 are present in amniotes.
source: Reciprocally, cyp2ae2 (FO904880.1) is clearly a member of the cyp2 family, and is likely orthologous to cyp2ae1 loci of other teleosts by sequence similarity and chromosomal position, yet no clear orthologues of this gene are present in amniotes (Ensembl Release 103) (Kirischian et al., 2011; Yates et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on database searches.

claim: The loss of red color in D. albolineatus erythrophores raises the possibility that CYP2J19 and Cyp2ae2 may have acquired carotenoid ketolase activity convergently.
source: The loss of red color in D. albolineatus erythrophores thus raises the possibility that CYP2J19 and Cyp2ae2 may have acquired carotenoid ketolase activity convergently.
evidence: Inferred from mutant phenotype and comparison to avian system.

claim: The cyp2ae2 mutant has markedly reduced amounts of astaxanthin in fin regions containing erythrophores but relatively greater amounts of zeaxanthin in both erythrophore and xanthophore containing tissue as compared to wild-type.
source: Supporting the idea that cyp2ae2 might encode a carotenoid ketolase, the cyp2ae2 mutant had markedly reduced amounts of astaxanthin in fin regions containing erythrophores but relatively greater amounts of zeaxanthin (peak 10) in both erythrophore and xanthophore containing tissue as compared to wild-type, consistent with cyp2ae2 expression in both tissues, albeit at different levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1—Table 5).
evidence: Result from HPLC analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1—Table 5.

claim: Erythrophores of cyp2ae2 mutants have markedly reduced red/green fluorescence ratios.
source: Consistent with these findings, erythrophores of cyp2ae2 mutants had markedly reduced red/green fluorescence ratios (Figure 7D)
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Erythrophores of cyp2ae2 mutants have a reduced diameter of visible pigment.
source: and a reduced diameter of visible pigment (Figure 7E).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The cyp2ae2 mutant allele cyp2ae2vp39ac1 harbors a five-nucleotide frameshift within the first coding exon leading to 42 novel amino acids followed by a premature stop codon (L46Δ43X).
source: Trace residual astaxanthin and other ketocarotenoids are unlikely to reflect residual activity of cyp2ae2, as the mutant allele, cyp2ae2vp39ac1, harbors a five-nucleotide frameshift within the first coding exon leading to 42 novel amino acids followed by a premature stop codon (L46Δ43X).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A paralogous locus, cyp2ae1, lies adjacent to cyp2ae2 and is expressed at very low levels in both fin regions.
source: A paralogous locus, cyp2ae1, lies adjacent to cyp2ae2 and was expressed at very low levels in both fin regions (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B; Supplementary file 1—Table 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B and RNA-seq data.

claim: Compensatory activity of cyp2ae1 might account for trace levels of ketocarotenoids in cyp2ae2vp39ac1.
source: Compensatory activity of cyp2ae1 might account for trace levels of ketocarotenoids in cyp2ae2vp39ac1.
evidence: Speculative explanation for residual ketocarotenoids in mutant.

claim: bdh1a encodes 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase type 1a, a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase.
source: The second red-deficient mutant, bdh1a, encodes 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase type 1a, a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase.
evidence: Based on gene annotation and homology.

claim: Homologues of bdh1a in mammals are known to interconvert hydroxyl and ketone groups, particularly acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate.
source: Homologues of this gene in mammals are known to interconvert hydroxyl and ketone groups, and in particular acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate, two major ketone bodies (Green et al., 1996; Langston et al., 1996; Persson et al., 2009; Otsuka et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Transcripts of a homologous gene to bdh1a were enriched in orange skin of clownfish Amphiprion ocellaris.
source: Although not implicated previously in carotenoid processing or red coloration, transcripts of a homologous gene were enriched in orange skin of clownfish Amphiprion ocellaris (Salis et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The bdh1a mutant completely lacks astaxanthin and other ketocarotenoids in erythrophore-containing tissue.
source: The bdh1avp40ac1 mutant (D141Δ12X) completely lacked astaxanthin and other ketocarotenoids in erythrophore-containing tissue, and did not exhibit increased levels of zeaxanthin, as observed in cyp2ae2vpa39c1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Result from HPLC analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Red/green fluorescence ratios of erythrophores in bdh1a mutants are similar to those of xanthophores.
source: Red/green fluorescence ratios of erythrophores are similar to those of xanthophores (Figure 7D)
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The diameter of visible pigment is reduced from wild-type levels in erythrophores of bdh1a mutants though not xanthophores.
source: and the diameter of visible pigment is reduced from wild-type levels in erythrophores though not xanthophores (Figure 7E), confirming the visible phenotype.
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Erythrophores of cyp2ae2 and bdh1a mutant fish appear normal in size and shape in young adults yet become morphologically heterogeneous as fish age.
source: Erythrophores of cyp2ae2 and bdh1a mutant fish appeared normal in size and shape in young adults yet became morphologically heterogeneous as fish age, with pigment-containing cell fragments and fewer cells evident, as well as an onset of whole-fish kyphosis by ~12 months post-fertilization (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Observed in older mutant fish shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C.

claim: cyp2ae2 and bdh1a are required for the accumulation of red carotenoids and subsequent homeostasis of erythrophores and other tissues.
source: These phenotypes suggest requirements for both loci in the accumulation of red carotenoids and subsequent homeostasis of erythrophores and other tissues, perhaps associated with a systemic dysregulation of carotenoid–Vitamin A—retinoid metabolism (von Lintig et al., 2005; Ghyselinck and Duester, 2019).
evidence: Inferred from mutant phenotypes, with reference to prior literature.

claim: β-carotene oxygenase 1 (Bco1) symmetrically cleaves β-carotene to produce vitamin A, a precursor of retinoic acid.
source: β-carotene oxygenase 1 (Bco1) symmetrically cleaves β-carotene to produce vitamin A, a precursor of retinoic acid; whereas β-carotene oxygenase 2 (Bco2) cleaves a variety of carotenoids in an asymmetric fashion, often leading to their degradation (Widjaja-Adhi et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017; Harrison and Kopec, 2020; Poliakov et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: β-carotene oxygenase 2 (Bco2) cleaves a variety of carotenoids in an asymmetric fashion, often leading to their degradation.
source: β-carotene oxygenase 1 (Bco1) symmetrically cleaves β-carotene to produce vitamin A, a precursor of retinoic acid; whereas β-carotene oxygenase 2 (Bco2) cleaves a variety of carotenoids in an asymmetric fashion, often leading to their degradation (Widjaja-Adhi et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017; Harrison and Kopec, 2020; Poliakov et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: bco1 and bco2b are more abundant in tissue containing xanthophores than erythrophores.
source: bco1 and bco2b were more abundant in tissue containing xanthophores than erythrophores (log2FC = 4.9, 2.1; q = 9.6E-23, 8.9E-8)
evidence: Result from RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: bco2l is similarly abundant at both erythrophore and xanthophore sites.
source: a third locus, bco2l was similarly abundant at both sites (Supplementary file 1—Table 1).
evidence: Result from RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Only bco1-targeted fish exhibited an overt pigmentary phenotype in F0 mosaic animals.
source: Only bco1-targeted fish exhibited an overt pigmentary phenotype in F0 mosaic animals, with pigment-free patches alongside patches of cells having apparently normal pigmentation consistent with a pigment-cell autonomous function (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Result from CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis screen shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Mutants carrying bco1 alleles have reduced carotenoid levels in both xanthophores and erythrophores.
source: Mutants stably carrying bco1 alleles (bco1vp41ac1, 52DΔ5X; bco1vp41ac2, 51FΔ9X) had reduced carotenoid levels in both xanthophores and erythrophores as well as smaller diameters of contracted pigment granules (Figure 7C–E; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Result from mutant analysis shown in Figure 7C-E.

claim: bco1 mutants have smaller diameters of contracted pigment granules.
source: Mutants stably carrying bco1 alleles (bco1vp41ac1, 52DΔ5X; bco1vp41ac2, 51FΔ9X) had reduced carotenoid levels in both xanthophores and erythrophores as well as smaller diameters of contracted pigment granules (Figure 7C–E; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The mechanism by which bco1 affects chromatophore carotenoid content remains unclear.
source: The mechanism of this effect on chromatophore carotenoid content remains unclear.
evidence: Stated as an open question following bco1 mutant analysis.

claim: In birds, carotenoids are concentrated in keratinocytes of the skin and displayed either directly or after incorporation into feathers.
source: In birds, carotenoids are concentrated in keratinocytes of the skin and displayed either directly or after incorporation into feathers (McGraw, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In ectotherms, carotenoids are concentrated in lipid droplets within pigment cells, chromatophores, visible through the epidermis and dermis.
source: In ectotherms, carotenoids are concentrated in lipid droplets within pigment cells, chromatophores, visible through the epidermis and dermis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carotenoid-based coloration in ectotherms.

claim: Red chromatophores are known as erythrophores, whereas yellow or orange chromatophores are referred to as xanthophores.
source: Red chromatophores are known as erythrophores, whereas yellow or orange chromatophores are referred to as xanthophores.
evidence: This is established terminology in the field.

claim: Both erythrophores and xanthophores can produce and retain pteridine pigments that sometimes also contribute to visible coloration.
source: Besides accumulating carotenoids, both cell types can produce and retain pteridine pigments that sometimes also contribute to visible coloration (Schartl et al., 2016; Parichy, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Erythrophores, xanthophores, and other skin chromatophores develop from embryonic neural crest cells.
source: Erythrophores and xanthophores, like other skin chromatophores—black melanophores, iridescent iridophores, and white leucophores—develop from embryonic neural crest cells, either directly, or indirectly, via latent progenitors in the peripheral nervous system or other tissue compartments (Kelsh et al., 2009; Patterson and Parichy, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In zebrafish, most xanthophores on the body differentiate as pteridine-containing xanthophores in the embryo, then proliferate and lose their color, only to reacquire carotenoid-dependent coloration in the adult.
source: In zebrafish for example, most xanthophores on the body differentiate as pteridine-containing xanthophores in the embryo, then proliferate and lose their color, only to reacquire carotenoid-dependent coloration in the adult; other xanthophores on the body and in the fin develop instead from latent progenitors (Tu and Johnson, 2011; McMenamin et al., 2014; Singh et al., 2016; Saunders et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Other xanthophores on the body and in the fin of zebrafish develop from latent progenitors.
source: In zebrafish for example, most xanthophores on the body differentiate as pteridine-containing xanthophores in the embryo, then proliferate and lose their color, only to reacquire carotenoid-dependent coloration in the adult; other xanthophores on the body and in the fin develop instead from latent progenitors (Tu and Johnson, 2011; McMenamin et al., 2014; Singh et al., 2016; Saunders et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The majority of adult iridophores and melanophores in zebrafish develop from a common progenitor in the peripheral nervous system.
source: By contrast, the majority of adult iridophores and melanophores develop from a common progenitor in the peripheral nervous system (Budi et al., 2011; Dooley et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A class of fin leucophore in zebrafish develops directly from melanophores.
source: Such transitions have long been known to be inducible experimentally (Niu, 1954; Ide and Hama, 1976), but have also been found naturally in zebrafish, in which a class of fin leucophore develops directly from melanophores (Lewis et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The analyses reveal striking parallels with the mechanism of red coloration in birds.
source: Our analyses are a first step toward defining the mechanisms underlying the development of erythrophore-mediated red coloration in Danio and reveal striking parallels with the mechanism of red coloration in birds.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Two loci required for, or associated with, ketocarotenoid accumulation have been identified in birds.
source: Likewise, the genes required for red coloration, as opposed to orange or yellow coloration, remain largely unexplored, although two loci required for, or associated with, ketocarotenoid accumulation, have been identified in birds (Lopes et al., 2016; Mundy et al., 2016; Toomey et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.
